item.title: Police raid leads to ASI and 5,000 yaba
item.description:
By bdnews24.com

Police have arrested an assistant sub-inspector (ASI) of Pallabi Police Station with 5,310 yaba pills for alleged involvement in drug trafficking.

ASI Md Shafiqul Islam, 43, and another man, known only as Wasim, 24, were arrested during overnight raids at Uttara’s Azampur.

Dakshinkhan Police chief Md Foyem Uddin confirmed the arrests to bdnews24.com.

He said police spotted Wasim trying to flee during a raid at Azampur Kachabazar and recovered 50 yaba pills from him.

Acting on his information, police raided a rented house and arrested Shafiqul with 200 yaba pills.

A subsequent raid on a flat at Noor Building in Bismillah Palli recovered another 5,110 pills, taking the total seizure to 5,310.

Investigating officer SI Shahinur Rahman said a case was filed under the Narcotics Control Act on Monday. Two to three unidentified people were also named.

A court later sent the two to jail.

The case statement says the suspects admitted during preliminary questioning that they brought yaba from different parts of the country and sold it in Dakshinkhan and surrounding areas.

Pallabi Police chief Hasan Bashir said Shafiqul joined the station about two months ago but had not performed duties there.

“We reported him absent to the station in June. He is not a good person,” he said.

item.title: Connecting Bhola and mainland by road
item.description:
By FE

The decision to establish road communication between the geographically isolated island district Bhola and the mainland deserves all-round appreciation. Dependent on only waterway connectivity, mobility of both people and goods is very slow which becomes slower still during inclement weather. The communication gets snapped in time of natural calamities. So, the proposed road link is going to change all such limitations and restrictions. Considering the island's economic potential particularly after the gas find and extraction, construction of a highway connecting Bhola, Barishal and Dhaka is overdue. The envisaged road communication through Hijla and Mehendiganj will drastically slash the travel time between Bhola and Dhaka via Barishal. When the people's mobility accelerates, economy gets a mighty boost. There is no reason why this will not happen in case of Bhola that has so long remained isolated to a large extent. 

In countries like Norway and Japan, even remote islands including those valued for their tourism have been brought under road and highway networks. Bhola may not be a tourist spot but the prospect of its marine resources, in addition to its gas reserve, is quite bright. It stands to be a hub of exploitation of what is called blue economy. So this investment in the proposed highway unfolds limitless possibilities of contribution of Bhola to the country's economy. Even the current status of the island is quite lofty with the haul of different fish species including Hilsha. Sure enough, commercial fishing awaits development not only in the waters around the island but also in the coastal belt in the country's southern districts. Road communications will help develop the marine fisheries and supply chain to the mutual benefits of inhabitants of Bhola and other districts including the capital city. 

Although no details have been furnished about the schedule of feasibility study and undertaking the project, the prime minister's insistence on accomplishment of the task gives a positive vibe. Now that the decision has been made, the ground works should be started as early as possible. Issues like financing of the project and tender floating should be completed within a reasonable time frame. It would be expected that the plan is executed within the term of this government. In a country where even bridges over rivers and canals with the potential of serving people of 10-20 villages are left half or partially done, any project of highway connecting Bhola with the mainland must not be left destined to similar fate. The faster it is started and completed the better. 

Greater emphasis on road communication to the neglect of the railway in defiance of logic has made the country pay heavily in terms of archaic connectivity, environment and costs. The proposed extension of highway connection up to Bhola does not fall under that category of road communication. But it should include an option for railway connectivity in the future when Barishal is brought under the rail network. The merit of developing mass transport instead of pressing into service imported luxurious buses cannot be disputed. But Bhola's case is special and road connectivity will serve the purpose well. Connecting the island district with the mainland will be a milestone achievement.

item.title: Govt must break the cycle of recruitment syndicates
item.description:
By Mir Mostafizur Rahaman

For Bangladesh, the reopening of the Malaysian labour market should be a source of hope. It should also be a test of whether the country has learnt the lessons of the past.

News that only 25 recruiting agencies may be allowed to send Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia has caused concern among recruitment companies and migrant rights advocates. Their fears are not difficult to understand. Bangladesh has already seen what can happen when access to a major overseas labour market is concentrated in the hands of a small number of intermediaries: recruitment costs rise, competition is weakened and migrant workers can end up paying the price.

Malaysia is too important a destination -- and overseas employment is too important to Bangladesh -- for the country to risk repeating those mistakes.

Bangladesh has around 2,500 licensed recruiting agencies. Many have years of experience in sending workers abroad. Restricting access to Malaysia to just 25 agencies therefore raises a basic question: on what grounds are these agencies being selected, and why should the rest be excluded?

If there are legitimate reasons to limit participation temporarily, the government should explain them publicly. The criteria should be transparent, independently verifiable and applied equally. Otherwise, a measure intended to streamline recruitment could instead create a new system of privilege.

The concern is particularly serious because of Malaysia's history as a destination for Bangladeshi migrant workers. Previous recruitment arrangements were dogged by allegations of syndication, excessive fees, irregularities and the exploitation of workers. A small group of agencies and intermediaries was accused of exercising disproportionate control over recruitment, leaving prospective migrants with little choice but to pay high fees to secure jobs.

The consequences were severe. Workers -- many of them from low-income households -- borrowed money, sold land or mortgaged property to finance their journeys. Some reportedly paid far more than the officially prescribed migration costs. A job that was supposed to improve a family's economic prospects could instead leave it heavily indebted.

This is precisely why transparency matters now.

The Malaysian labour market is not simply another destination for Bangladeshi workers. It is one of the country's most important overseas employment markets. For decades, Malaysia has offered jobs to Bangladeshis in plantations, manufacturing, construction and services. A properly managed Malaysian market can provide thousands of workers with regular employment and a pathway to better incomes.

It also matters to the wider Bangladeshi economy.

Overseas workers are among the country's most important economic assets. Every year, millions of Bangladeshis working abroad send money home to their families. Remittances support household spending, education, healthcare and housing, while providing a crucial source of foreign currency for the country.

The importance of remittances becomes particularly clear when Bangladesh faces pressure on its external accounts. Money sent home by migrant workers helps strengthen the country's foreign-exchange position and supports economic stability. For millions of families, meanwhile, remittances are not an abstract macroeconomic statistic but the money that pays for food, school fees, medical treatment or the construction of a home.

Yet the contribution of migrant workers often begins with a considerable financial burden.

The cost of leaving the country can be extraordinarily high. Recruitment fees, travel expenses, medical tests, training and payments to intermediaries can consume a large portion of a worker's expected earnings. When recruitment is controlled by a small number of agencies, the possibility of excessive charges becomes greater, particularly where workers have few alternatives.

That is why the government should resist any arrangement that creates unnecessary concentration in the recruitment business.

There is a difference between regulation and restriction. The government has every right -- and indeed a responsibility -- to ensure that only competent and trustworthy agencies recruit workers for Malaysia. Agencies with records of malpractice should not be allowed to participate. But that objective does not necessarily require creating a closed group of 25 agencies.

A better approach would be a transparent accreditation system. Agencies could be assessed on their record, financial capacity, compliance with regulations, experience, worker-protection mechanisms and history of complaints. Those that meet clearly defined standards could be allowed to participate, while agencies that fail could be excluded.

Such a system would create competition without sacrificing oversight.

The recruitment process should also become far more transparent to the workers themselves. Before leaving Bangladesh, a migrant should know exactly how much the job will cost, who is paying which part of the recruitment expenses, what salary has been agreed, where the worker will live and what happens if the promised job does not materialise.

The government could publish approved recruitment costs and employer information online and require all payments to be made through traceable channels. Digital registration and complaint mechanisms could reduce the role of informal brokers, who often operate in the shadows of the formal recruitment system.

The agreement between Bangladesh and Malaysia should also be judged by what it delivers to workers, rather than simply by the number of people sent abroad.

A successful labour migration arrangement should guarantee that workers receive contracts they understand, wages that are paid on time, safe accommodation, access to healthcare and effective mechanisms for resolving disputes. It should also contain safeguards against contract substitution, forced labour and other forms of exploitation.

The government should make these protections central to its negotiations with Malaysia.

There is another reason for caution. Bangladesh is competing with other labour-sending countries for access to Malaysia and other international markets. If Bangladeshi workers become associated with high recruitment costs, opaque intermediaries and complicated procedures, Bangladesh risks losing its competitiveness.

A more transparent system, by contrast, could become a selling point. If Bangladeshi workers can be recruited at reasonable cost, through accountable agencies and under clear contracts, both workers and employers stand to benefit.

There should be no room for backroom deals or opaque decision-making.

The government must also establish strong monitoring mechanisms after recruitment begins. Transparency at the selection stage will mean little if agencies are subsequently allowed to charge workers excessive fees or use unregistered brokers. Regular audits, worker feedback, public disclosure of recruitment costs and swift penalties for violations should form part of the system.

Most importantly, migrant workers must not be treated simply as a source of remittances.

They are citizens whose labour sustains families and contributes to the national economy. They deserve a migration system that protects their dignity as well as their earnings.

Malaysia has the potential to become an important destination for a new generation of Bangladeshi workers. But reopening that market should not mean reopening the door to the practices that damaged it before.

Bangladesh has an opportunity to build something better: a recruitment system based on transparency, competition and accountability, where legitimate agencies compete on quality and compliance rather than access to political or administrative privilege.

The choice should be clear. Bangladesh needs more jobs abroad, but it does not need more middlemen. It needs higher remittances, but not at the cost of workers being pushed into debt. And it needs a Malaysian labour market that is open and sustainable, not one controlled by a handful of powerful interests.

The lessons of the past should not be forgotten. If the Malaysian labour market is to reopen, it must reopen in a way that puts Bangladeshi workers first.

item.title: As dreams are made on....
item.description:
By Nilratan Halder

"We are such stuff as dreams are made on, and our little life is rounded with sleep"-so does Shakespeare view human life. But then what are dreams made of? Science is yet to unravel this mystery. However, in his book Interpretation of Dreams, Sigmund Freud claims that dreams are 'disguised fulfilments of repressed and unconscious wishes'. According to him, dreams allow the unconscious mind 'to safely express forbidden desires, aggressive urges or childhood impulses that are rejected by the conscious mind'.

No doubt there is a process for sorting out memories of what people experience during their daily exchange with each other or observe in a given situation. Not all things are retained in memory but a few things stay stuck. Those things and events form the basis of dreams. Some of the dreams are almost a true representation of what happened in daily life. People in such cases can easily connect their dreams with the practical things or events confronted or experienced in the conscious state of mind. In most such cases, the representation happens with some alterations or modifications. Particularly, where emotional affairs such as love, hatred, violence, friendliness, shock, repulsion etc.; are involved, the images are reconstructed authentically or edited or given a new shape according to the mental makeup of the observers.

There is no knowing what stimulates the mind to call back the recent images or those that happened years or decades ago or even in childhood. Some that left a deep impression on minds can even repeat. But what about dreams almost surreal with no connection with everyday life's experiences? Yes, some of these dreams can look like as if they are from a different world. A natural scene painted on the canvas of dream with such a strong impression that its dreamers can recollect with ease. The scene formed in a dream is preserved as a lasting impression for the whole life. This can be static or like a reel unfolding in its magnificence.

Sure enough, the kinds of dreams people dream vary depending on their mentality. Similar things can happen when people are awake. Visualising a beautiful picture with no reference to any place in real life is a most enjoyable experience. For example, a small woodland located on the fringe of an expansive field where the undulating young rice plants make perfect picture for the inner eye. The woodland developed on a raised platform of soil has on its slope vegetables cultivated sparsely. There is a fence of bamboo that is no longer intact. Overall, the details of the scene are more realistic than any real place. Wonder of wonders, there is no existence of this scene in real world; it exists only in the beholder's mind.

If a place visited appears in a dream, it is quite natural. But when in a conscious state of mind such a beautiful picture gets created, it is indeed an artistic exploration. The creation of such soothing images in a dream too is more like a spiritual experience. Most dreams are forgotten immediately afterwards, some stays for hours or days but those that leave a deep impression are a treasure trove for people who behold those.

Of course, there are nightmares. Some are so violent and repulsive that those force a dreamer awake in a state of delusion. The persons may shout or ask for help as they get up and struggle to come out of the spell. It is like hallucination. In this connection, there are tales of football-playing husbands kicking their spouses out of bed. There are many such funny incidents that occur because the thin line between reality and illusion created by dreams at times vanishes. Some people really need help from sleeping partners or members of their families to come to their senses.

Dreams are not real but they can be a reflection of the real world. Many people claim they sleep deeply and do not dream at all. That is a lie because dream is an indispensable element that helps maintain a balance between the real life full of stress and strain and the world of the unknown. The fact is that they cannot remember the dreams. Dreams release tensions and after a peaceful sleep, one feel refreshed. Let your dream not make you kick your sleeping partner out of bed but turn you a better person under its soothing influences.
item.author: Nilratan Halder

item.title: How Gen Z is faring in the changed context
item.description:
By Nilratan Halder

Unravelling the minds of Millennials, Generation Z or Gen Z and Generation Alpha is no easy task. But some streaks common in one generation differentiate it from the other two. The Millennials had their time when life was relatively quieter but now it is the Gen Z which rules the roost. This generation is more vocal compared to the preceding one and is bold enough to confront the authorities. The Generation Alpha is yet to take over from the Gen Z and how they emerge will be quite interesting to observe. About one thing, though, there is no doubt that the Millennials and the Gen Z are not happy with the way the old guards in power govern. While the former was displeased and yet did not take the initiative to launch organised protests against the authorities, the latter dare call the spade a spade.

In Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal and India, the Gen Z has demonstrated its organising power far stronger than any political party. Momentous changes have already been brought about or the process is on the roll. Belying the tag that this generation is self-centred, hooked on computer and smartphone screens and reluctant to take responsibility, this generation is responding to the call of duty. Unlike political parties, the members of this generation are focused to the social ills and discriminations. Sure enough, they have changed the social perception of well-being of the common people, particularly those at the lowest tier of society. But can they complete the process? That is the million-dollar question.

The mainstream of the Gen Z in this region appears to have lost the momentum after their initial success. To achieve the ultimate objective, they must not get involved with the traditional system of politics. If they compromise on radical socio-economic reform, the movement falter while disappointing the deprived segments of society. Sure enough, a section of their own generation which is hardly educated and politically conscious joined the movement in the hope of changing their lot. That hope is now fading in the distant horizon in one or two countries in South Asia. The split in their organisation over some contentious issues shows that things are going off track.

In a situation like this, the rift has already weakened their organisations and more importantly their moral standing. Many feel they have been let down. It is not only them but the well-meaning citizens are disappointed. In the absence of any socio-economic programme, the not-so-educated-and-skilled among them will revert to the screen or other self-annihilating addictions. But the highly educated and talented among them will look for better options. Irrespective of generations, this cream crop of society will look for avenues to leave this country for higher studies and settle abroad.

In fact, the more talented young people, irrespective of the generations they belong to, have tried their luck in Western countries. They consider, there is no future in this country. There is no point wasting their talent in their native countries where they cannot make use of their merit and ambition. When the mediocre rule the roost, they find themselves neglected. This is a hard truth and no government has been interested to create the creative environment for them to stay back or return after completion of studies abroad. Brain drain, as it is called, has continued unabated depriving the service of bright and inventive minds. Foreign countries have made provision for absorbing them in research and invention projects.

Although, US President Donald Trump has been making immigration laws stringent, the geniuses from around the world are unlikely to face any opposition to stay in the United States of America. Other countries in Europe and North America also are not averse to following the same rule. A few of the bright minds like Dr. Muhammed Zafar Iqbal returned home leaving behind high salaried jobs and opportunities for research in USA only to be maligned now. Narrow and partisan politics has implicated him in crimes a man of his stature is unlikely to commit.

Why will Bangladesh-born scientists and other successful diaspora come back? If a nation cannot cultivate geniuses and resourceful minds at home, the loss is no one else's but its own. To develop scientifically and culturally, the nation must respect the sons and daughters of this soil, who excel others in various fields. Economy will follow once that criterion is fulfilled.

item.title: Growing cashless retail payments through Bangla QR
item.description:
By Shahadat Khan

Over the past decade, Bangladesh has made impressive progress in digital financial services. More than 90 million active mobile financial service accounts are now in use, processing around 22 million transactions worth nearly Tk 6,000 crore on an average day. People regularly cash in and cash out at agent points, send money, receive salaries and government benefits, recharge mobile phones, and pay utility bills.

Yet walk into any grocery store or pharmacy, and the picture changes completely. Digital payments for everyday retail purchases have lagged far behind other financial use cases. Cash still accounts for more than 98% of retail transactions in Bangladesh. Money enters the digital system daily, but much of it is cashed out again before it is ever spent. Customers pay a cash-out charge just to withdraw their own money, merchants go back to carrying and counting notes at the end of the day, and the country loses the efficiency it has worked so hard to build across the digital financial system. The last mile - the actual moment of paying for groceries, medicine or a meal - has stayed almost entirely analogue.

Bangladesh Bank has recognised this gap and is now working with renewed urgency to popularise Bangla QR, the country's interoperable QR standard. It allows customers to pay participating merchants through a single, unified QR code, regardless of the bank or wallet used by either party. To support this push and give it a coherent shape, we propose a simple 4P framework: Presence, Performance, Promotion and Pricing.

Presence - Bangla QR should be visible at merchant points across the country, and customers' mobile apps should clearly show the Bangla QR option. Codes need to be displayed prominently at the counter, not tucked away, and the scan option should sit on the home screen of every banking and wallet app rather than buried in a menu.

Performance - payments must work reliably, with a clear success-rate target and fast resolution when they don't. Customers and merchants judge the whole system by what happens at the counter, so failures need to be rare and, when they do happen, resolved within minutes rather than days.

Promotion - once the first two are solid, campaigns and incentives can build the habit of paying by QR. This includes customer and merchant awareness drives, cashback or reward-based incentives, and government institutions leading by example so people see Bangla QR used everywhere they go.

Pricing - over time, the merchant cost needs to come down to a level that makes digital payment genuinely attractive against cash. That means testing real transaction data, comparing it against what merchants pay today, and adjusting rates so cost is never the reason a shop turns away a digital payment.

The sequencing of this work matters. Presence and Performance form the Prepare phase - without these two working properly, the market isn't ready to move forward. Promotion and Pricing then form the Growth phase, where adoption is meant to accelerate.

Presence: real progress since June

On Presence, June brought solid progress. Bangladesh's major providers have now switched their merchants over to Bangla QR - proprietary QR codes that banks and MFS operators used to issue on their own have been replaced with the unified standard, and the change is visible inside the apps themselves. The country already has more than 15 lakh Bangla QR merchants. From 1 July, the government has made a Bangla QR code mandatory for trade licence renewal, which will bring in many more. Banks are also moving: each bank is working to onboard merchants for QR accounts, with individual branches targeting around 100 new merchant accounts each. At this pace, we could see well over 10 lakh additional QR merchants within a few months. On the customer side, the major wallets and banking apps - including bKash and Nagad - have all added a Bangla QR payment option.

Performance: now is the time

to focus here

With Presence advancing, it is time to focus on the second P: Performance. We need to be confident that Bangla QR payments work reliably. If 1,000 customers try to pay at 1,000 different shops today, at least 970 of those payments should succeed - a 97% success rate. If more than 10% of payment attempts fail, customers and merchants will become frustrated and lose confidence in Bangla QR. Once lost, that confidence will be difficult to regain.

Real-time, in-person payments carry a particular kind of pressure that bank transfers don't. Picture a customer paying Tk 3,000 for baby formula for his child. His account is deducted, but the merchant does not receive the payment - and he is told the issue will take three months to resolve. That simply cannot be the standard. When a payment fails after the customer's account has been debited, the funds should be released or refunded automatically within minutes in most cases.

Bangladesh Bank has already introduced a Transaction Status Inquiry (TSI) service for the Bangla QR platform. A provider like bKash can check the status within a minute, and if the merchant's provider confirms the payment was never received, refund the customer immediately. This needs to be monitored daily - how many such cases occur, and how quickly they are resolved. Done properly, TSI should be able to resolve the vast majority of these cases automatically within three minutes.

Growth phase: promotion and pricing

Once Presence and Performance are solid, we should expect a major jump in cashless transactions. This is when campaigns should begin - educating both customers and merchants on the benefits of Bangla QR, and offering incentives for going digital. One idea worth exploring: if micro-merchants could process their everyday Tk 200-300 transactions at no cost, it could meaningfully increase transaction volumes at exactly the level where cash is hardest to displace.

On pricing, we may operate and observe Bangla QR for two to three months before revisiting the numbers. For many low-margin merchants, an MDR of 1% may still be too high. Over time, stakeholders should work together to bring the MDR closer to 0.5%. Three months of operating data-covering transaction patterns, merchant costs and provider revenue-should provide a sound basis for designing a fairer and more sustainable pricing structure.

The government's push on Bangla QR is timely. If we execute the 4P framework - Presence and Performance first, then Promotion and Pricing - we can turn this into a genuine shift in how Bangladesh pays. That means more digital transactions, deeper financial inclusion, greater economic empowerment for ordinary people, and faster overall economic growth.

Shahadat Khan, Ph.D., is the Founder and CEO of TallyKhata and TallyPay.

item.title: Nordic nations say they have lost confidence in Infantino and FIFA governance
item.description:
By REUTERS

Six Nordic football associations delivered a united blow to FIFA President Gianni Infantino on Sunday, declaring they had lost confidence in his leadership while demanding sweeping governance reforms at world football's governing body.

The six Nordic FIFA members -- Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and the Faroe Islands -- met in Helsinki and issued a rare joint statement backing calls for Infantino's resignation from three major regional confederations.

They also supported demands for an independent investigation into his controversial proposal to sell a stake in events like the World Cup to private equity investors, a plan that was quickly abandoned in the face of global backlash.

"The six Nordic football associations have lost confidence in FIFA's president and are concerned about the organisation's governance and decision-making at the highest level," they said in a statement.

"The Nordic football associations stand united with UEFA and support the measures that the organisation and its national member associations have jointly proposed.

"We expect FIFA to provide binding guarantees that the organisation's governance or competitions will never again be opened up to private ownership."

Reuters has contacted FIFA for comment on the statement.

On Friday, Denmark's football association (DBU) vowed to find a credible alternative to Infantino in next year's election.

Infantino is under pressure from three confederations to resign, including Europe's UEFA, Asia's AFC and CONCACAF, which represents North and Central America and the Caribbean.

The sport's regional powerhouses have also discussed a potential vote of no confidence against the FIFA chief.

"We also support the demand made by AFC, CONCACAF and UEFA that a fully independent external investigation into the events surrounding the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal be established," the Nordic FAs added.

"We also call on FIFA to initiate a comprehensive and independent review of its governance framework to determine whether it ensures the independence, checks and balances, transparency and accountability that were intended when FIFA adopted its reform programme in 2016."

Infantino, who is seeking a fourth term until 2031 at next year's election, is in the Dominican Republic this weekend where he met with officials of the Caribbean Football Union.

CONCACAF President Victor Montagliani had asked Infantino to stay away from a youth soccer tournament in the country, saying his presence would overshadow the event.

"This meeting of the Presidents of CFU takes place in the environment of (a) Under-14 youth tournament in the region, which actually is one of those tournaments that can take place thanks (to) the FIFA Forward programme," Infantino said.

"So, even more so, a reason to be proud to be here. And happy, as well, because it's important to engage, to have a dialogue, to express views and opinions."

item.title: Bangladesh climb to their highest-ever No. 6 in Test rankings despite heavy defeat
item.description:
By bdnews24.com

Bangladesh’s heavy defeat in the second Test has done little to blunt the impact of their historic win in Darwin.

The series-ending ICC rankings update has rewarded that breakthrough victory, lifting the Tigers to their highest-ever position in Test cricket.

After 26 years of Test cricket, the men in red and green have climbed to No. 6 for the first time.

Their rise to sixth was secured immediately after the win over the top-ranked side in Darwin. The post-series update has now officially confirmed it.

Bangladesh’s previous best was seventh, achieved after a 2-0 series sweep of Pakistan in May. They later slipped after losing the series in Zimbabwe.

Najmul Hossain Shanto’s side started the series with 73 rating points. After the drawn series, they have 78, moving above Pakistan on 75 and Sri Lanka on 76.

Australia remain at the summit despite losing in Darwin. Their rating, however, has fallen from 131 to 126.

South Africa are second with 119 points, followed by New Zealand on 106 and India on 104. England, above Bangladesh, have 99.

Bangladesh’s best ODI ranking is also sixth, first achieved by Mashrafe Bin Mortaza’s team in May 2017. Their best T20I ranking was fourth in July 2012, when the rankings were still relatively new.
item.author: bdnews24.com

item.title: Shoriful bags maiden Test five-for to lead Bangladesh fightback
item.description:
By bdnews24.com

Shoriful Islam marked his return from injury with his maiden Test five-wicket haul as Bangladesh produced a spirited response after being bowled out for just 64 by Australia in Mackay.

The left-arm seamer struck twice in an over for the second time in the innings, removing Beau Webster and captain Pat Cummins to leave Australia 146-7 after 32 overs on the opening day of the second and final Test.

Cameron Green remained at the crease alongside Mitchell Starc, with Australia having moved 82 runs ahead of Bangladesh’s first-innings total.

Shoriful, recalled to the side after recovering from a hamstring injury, had earlier dismissed Travis Head and Marnus Labuschagne in quick succession before tea.

His fourth wicket was the prized scalp of Steve Smith, who had helped Australia recover from 41-3 in a 77-run partnership with Green.

Smith, who made 42 from 74 balls with six fours, was trapped lbw by a superb Shoriful delivery that pitched on off stump and straightened.

The former Australia captain reviewed the decision, but both impact and the ball hitting the stumps were shown as umpire’s call, leaving the on-field decision to stand.

Mehidy Hasan Miraz then struck with his first over of the innings, having Alex Carey caught by Hasan Mahmud at mid-on for five.

Shoriful returned to take centre stage.

Webster was given lbw first ball to a delivery that pitched on off stump and would have gone on to hit it. His review could not save him, sending him back for a golden duck.

One ball later, Cummins was unable to negotiate a sharp bouncer. The ball took his glove as he attempted to defend and looped through to wicketkeeper Litton Das, giving Shoriful his fifth wicket.

It completed a remarkable turnaround for the 25-year-old after Bangladesh endured a disastrous start to the match.

Australia captain Cummins had elected to bowl on a lively surface at the Great Barrier Reef Arena, which became the country’s 12th Test venue.

Starc then tore through Bangladesh’s top order, taking the first five wickets as the tourists collapsed to 12-5 inside seven overs.

The left-arm quick struck with the first ball of the Test to remove Shadman Islam and went on to dismiss Tanzid Hasan, Najmul Hossain Shanto, Mominul Haque and Litton.

Starc eventually finished with 6-12, while Cummins took 3-25 as Bangladesh were dismissed for 64.

Shoriful, batting at number 10, made 14 before becoming Starc’s sixth victim.

But he soon made a far greater impact with the ball.

Australia reached tea on 50-3 after Taskin Ahmed removed recalled opener Matt Renshaw for eight and Shoriful accounted for Head and Labuschagne.

Smith and Green then rebuilt the innings before Shoriful returned to break the partnership and lead Bangladesh’s fightback.

Bangladesh lead the two-Test series 1-0 after a nine-wicket victory in the opener in Darwin.
item.author: bdnews24.com

item.title: Starc takes six as Bangladesh bowled out for 64
item.description:
By UNB

Mitchell Starc took 6 for 12 as Bangladesh were bowled out for 64 in 34 overs on Saturday, giving Australia a commanding start to the second Test in Mackay.

Bangladesh lost five wickets for 12 runs after Australia opted to field, with four of their top six batters dismissed without scoring.

Shadman Islam was out to the first ball, edging Starc to Cameron Green at gully.

Tanzid Hasan followed for a duck in Starc’s second over, and two balls later Najmul Hossain Shanto was trapped lbw.

Mominul Haque made 9 before edging Starc to Green, while Litton Das was given out lbw after Australia successfully reviewed the decision. Mushfiqur Rahim, the other batter among the top six to score, made 5 before Pat Cummins bowled him.

Bangladesh were 35 for 6 at lunch. Mehidy Hasan Miraz, who made 11, and Hasan Mahmud added some resistance before Australia’s attack finished the innings in the afternoon.

The only partnership of more than 20 came at the end. Taijul Islam and Shoriful Islam put on 25 for the 10th wicket, the best stand of Bangladesh’s innings. Shoriful made 14 from 19 balls, with three fours, while Taijul was unbeaten on 11.

Starc returned to dismiss Shoriful caught behind for his sixth wicket.

Cummins took 3 for 25 and Josh Hazlewood 1 for 18. Starc bowled 10 overs, six of them maidens.

Hazlewood said there was movement in the air and off the pitch early in the innings, with the breeze helping the swing. He also felt the surface became flatter later in the innings.

Australia, beaten by nine wickets in Darwin, now have a chance to take a firm grip on the match and level the two-Test series.
